question: how do I review pull requests?
fact: Reviews PRs by reading the diff, never trusting the description.
native_answer:
Two ways, depending on whose code it is.

Reviewing someone else's PR (the usual case)
1. Context first, but skeptically: gh pr view <n> --comments, gh pr diff <n> --name-only, gh pr checks <n>. Read the description last — it's a claim, the diff is the fact.
2. Check it out so you can read files, not just hunks: git fetch origin pull/<n>/head:pr-<n> && git checkout pr-<n>
3. Read the full diff against base: git diff main...HEAD, then file-by-file for anything non-obvious, opening the surrounding file with read_file where the diff alone doesn't show you enough context.
4. Run it: the test suite and the linter locally, plus anything the PR claims to fix. A green CI badge is not evidence you verified.
5. Checklist, in order of what actually blocks merge: correctness and edge cases (empty/null/concurrent), security (secrets in the diff, input validation, SQL/shell injection, authz), tests (new paths covered, error cases too), then quality/performance/docs as non-blocking.
6. Post it: a formal review with the verdict, plus inline comments on the specific lines. gh pr review <n> --approve | --request-changes --comment, or one atomic API call to /pulls/<n>/reviews with a comments[] array so all the inline notes land in a single review.
7. Clean up: git checkout main && git branch -D pr-<n>

Approve only when there are no critical or warning-level findings; request changes for anything that should be fixed pre-merge; comment if it's a draft or you're not sure.

Reviewing your own changes before pushing
git diff main...HEAD --stat, then the full diff, same checklist, findings presented as Critical / Warnings / Suggestions / Looks Good. Different from a PR review: this one is about not pushing the mistake, so it's worth grepping the diff for leftover print/console.log, TODO/FIXME, conflict markers, and anything secret-shaped.

One environment note: gh isn't installed on this box (command not found), so PR-level work here falls back to the GitHub REST API with a token, or plain git for anything local — `git fetch origin pull/<n>/head` needs no gh at all.

    gh pr diff 123 --name-only

and to deliver the review:

question: how do I back up my personal files?
fact: Backs up to a USB SSD monthly, no cloud backup for personal files.
native_answer:
Your setup — monthly copy to a USB SSD — is one copy on one medium, and a monthly cadence means a worst case of losing a month of work. Two things are worth fixing: make it versioned rather than a mirror, and get a third copy somewhere that isn't your apartment.

Short version: Time Machine for the whole boot volume, restic for personal files onto the USB SSD, and a second restic repo on the N100 over the VPN. No cloud, three copies, two of them off the laptop.

Why not just rsync-to-the-SSD: a mirror propagates deletions instantly, so "I deleted the wrong folder three weeks ago" and "the SSD got corrupted mid-copy" both become unrecoverable. You want snapshots with retention, not a mirror.

The recipe, on the Mac (restic is currently 0.19.x, `brew install restic`):

    export RESTIC_REPOSITORY=/Volumes/BackupSSD/restic
    export RESTIC_PASSWORD_FILE=~/.config/restic/pw   # chmod 600
    restic init
    restic backup ~/Documents ~/Pictures ~/Projects --exclude-file ~/.config/restic/excludes.txt

into `excludes.txt` put the noise: `Library/Caches`, `node_modules`, `*.tmp`, `.venv`, browser profile dirs. Then set retention so the repo doesn't grow forever:

    restic forget --keep-daily 7 --keep-weekly 5 --keep-monthly 12 --prune
    restic check --read-data-subset=5%

The second repo goes on the home server, reachable over your VPN when you're away — that's your offsite copy and it needs no cloud vendor:

    export RESTIC_REPOSITORY=sftp:you@n100:/srv/backup/restic
    restic init && restic backup ~/Documents ~/Pictures ~/Projects

Same password file, same excludes. Run the laptop-local backup daily via a launchd plist, the server one nightly too — you're on that VPN most of the time anyway. Bump the SSD from monthly to weekly, and physically unplug it between runs; a drive that stays mounted is not an offline copy, it's just another disk that ransomware and `rm -rf` can reach.

The part people skip: a backup you haven't restored from isn't a backup. Once a quarter, `restic restore latest --target /tmp/verify --include /Documents/somefile` and confirm the file opens. `restic check` proves the repo is internally consistent, not that your restore path works.

One caveat on restic for the first run: it dedupes and chunks, so the initial backup of a 1TB disk over sftp will take hours. Do the first server-side run at home over the LAN, then let the incremental runs handle the VPN.

The fix, in order of payoff:

Make the frequent copy automatic instead of monthly. Time Machine to a dedicated drive (or over the network to the N100, which is reachable through your VPN) gives you hourly snapshots of everything with no decisions to make. That alone closes the "month of lost work" hole.

For the subset that actually matters — documents, photos, your plain-text notes, dotfiles — use restic or borg to the home server, running nightly from a LaunchAgent. Both are boring, proven, and give you encrypted, deduplicated, versioned snapshots, so a stolen drive or server compromise isn't also a data leak. Your dotfiles bare git repo just needs a second remote on the Forgejo instance plus one offsite mirror; that's a one-line change and it's already the right design.

The offsite copy is the genuinely missing piece. Either rotate a second SSD to Berlin or a desk drawer at work, or point restic at an encrypted object store (Backblaze B2, Hetzner, S3). Deduplicated personal data is usually small enough that this costs a few euros a month at most.

Two traps to avoid: encrypt the portable SSD as an APFS encrypted volume, and keep the restic passphrase somewhere outside the machine and outside the backup — an unrecoverable passphrase turns a working backup into noise. Then actually verify:

    restic check --read-data-subset=5%
    restic restore latest --include ~/Documents/some-file --target /tmp/restore-test

Run that check monthly and restore one real file every quarter.

Set up and verified working at /root/finance — a plain-text double-entry ledger on hledger (1.50.3, installed via apt on this box).

How it works: you drop the month's bank CSV in inbox/, run `sh scripts/import.sh`, then `sh scripts/report.sh`. hledger remembers which rows it has already seen (`.latest.<file>` markers beside each CSV), so re-running is a no-op — I confirmed that with three months of sample data. All state is text: main.journal includes accounts.journal, budget.journal and journal/*.journal.

Real output from the sample run, not a mock-up. September: expenses EUR 1.841,12 against a net of EUR 2.350,00; home EUR 1.338,19 (rent 1.250 + utilities 88,19), travel EUR 184,00 which is 123% of its EUR 150 target, fuel EUR 121,00 at 101% of EUR 120. The report ends with the postings still sitting in expenses:unknown, which is the only recurring chore — each one is either a rule to add to rules/generic.rules or a one-off edit in journal/imported.journal.

Two things I got wrong first and corrected against the tool rather than the docs, both now documented in the README because they'll bite you too:

- In hledger 1.x the last matching `if` block in a CSV rules file wins, not the first. I proved it by listing `GALP` as fuel and `GALP GAS` as a utility in both orders — the later block always won. So broad patterns go on top, exceptions below.
- Rules only apply at import time. The September `LOJA DA ESQUINA` row stays in unknown after I added the grocery rule in October, which is exactly why the correction path is editing the journal.

Also: the bank account is declared `type: C` rather than `A`, because `hledger cashflow` silently reports zeros for anything not marked liquid.

Files: README.md (prose, explains the whole design), main.journal, accounts.journal, budget.journal, rules/generic.rules, scripts/import.sh, scripts/report.sh, journal/2026.journal plus a sample inbox/ with three months of Lisbon-flavoured exports.

Two leftovers I could not remove in this unattended session — the security policy blocks `rm` in root paths: bin/ (66MB of wrong-architecture hledger binaries I downloaded before discovering this host is aarch64) and tmp/ (the four rules files from the precedence experiment). Delete them with `rm -rf /root/finance/bin /root/finance/tmp /root/finance/unpack.py`.

On your own machines: `brew install hledger` on the Mac, `apt install hledger` on the N100 box, then copy this directory over. The one thing you must adapt is the layout block at the top of rules/generic.rules — skip/separator/decimal-mark/date-format/fields have to match your bank's export exactly. Check it with `hledger print -f inbox/yourfile.csv` before importing; it prints the accounts the rules would produce and writes nothing. I saved the whole workflow as the `plain-text-spending-ledger` skill, with the scripts and layout in its references, so this is repeatable next time.

You already do this — a plain spreadsheet, deliberately no budgeting app — which is the right call given the de-Googled phone and the self-hosted, plain-text setup you otherwise run. So the real question is whether to improve that workflow or replace it.

The spreadsheet itself is fine. The failure mode isn't the format, it's drift: manual entry gets skipped for a couple of weeks, the totals stop matching the bank, and the sheet quietly becomes fiction. Two things actually fix that.

The low-effort route is to keep the sheet and add a monthly reconciliation. Once a month you export CSV or OFX from each account, run something small on the Debian box that normalises the columns and appends the rows, then you tick the closing balance against the statement. That's maybe 40 lines of Python and it turns "did I remember to log it" into "does the number match" — a question with a yes/no answer.

The bigger route is plain-text accounting with hledger or ledger: transactions as text files in git (you're already comfortable with bare-git dotfiles), double-entry, and hledger's CSV import with rules files that absorbs recurring bank exports without you retyping anything. It runs comfortably on the N100. The cost is a genuine learning curve, and double-entry is overkill if all you want to know is what you spent on groceries.
